facts: Andromeda was a princess chained to a rock as a sacrifice to the sea monster Cetus, until Perseus rescued her — her mother Cassiopeia's boasting caused the whole affair. Its Great Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is the most distant object visible to the unaided eye, about 2.5 million light years away.

Antlia was created in the 1750s by French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille, who named 14 southern constellations after scientific instruments. It celebrates the air pump invented by Robert Boyle in 1659.

Apus, 'the bird of paradise', was named by Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman around 1600 after birds brought back from New Guinea. The name literally means 'footless' in Greek, because bird-of-paradise skins arrived with feet removed — a legend said they never landed.
Aquarius the Water Bearer is one of the oldest constellations, linked by Babylonians to their water god. His jar, Aquarius sits near Pegasus and pours water toward the bright star Fomalhaut.

Aquila is the eagle of Zeus who carried his thunderbolts and, in myth, retrieved the Trojan boy Ganymede to serve the gods. Its brightest star Altair, with Vega and Deneb, forms the famous Summer Triangle.

Ara, the Altar, marks the altar where the gods swore the oath that started the war against the Titans. Lacaille trimmed its tail in the 1700s, moving the star cluster NGC 6397 into neighbouring Norma.
Aries, the Ram, is the golden-fleeced ram that carried the children Phrixus and Helle. Its brightest star, Hamal, is nearly identical to the Sun but 65 light years away.
Auriga the Charioteer is often shown carrying a goat on his arm — the star Capella is Latin for 'little she-goat'. Its Flaming Star Nebula is a dramatic red cloud lit by the young star AE Aurigae.
Boötes the Herdsman holds a club and leash while chasing the Great Bear around the pole. Arcturus, its brightest star, was the first star seen in daylight through a telescope, in 1634.
Caelum, 'the chisel', is one of Lacaille's instrument constellations from the 1750s. It has no stars brighter than 4th magnitude and no famous objects — one of the faintest constellations in the sky.
Camelopardalis is one of the faintest constellations, created by Petrus Plancius in 1613. It sits near the north pole and contains Kemble's Cascade, a striking chain of more than 20 stars.

Cancer the Crab was sent by Hera to nip at Heracles during his fight with the Hydra; the goddess rewarded its efforts with a place in the sky. Inside it is the Beehive Cluster (M44), visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy patch.

Canes Venatici was created by Johannes Hevelius in 1687, splitting the 'jackals' between Ursa Major and Boötes. Cor Caroli ('Charles's Heart'), its brightest star, was named in honour of King Charles II of England.
Canis Major contains Sirius, the brightest star in the entire night sky — only 8.6 light years away. In ancient Egypt the rising of Sirius announced the Nile flood.

Canis Minor is 'the Lesser Dog', known in Greek as Procyon, 'before the dog', because it rises before Sirius. Procyon means the brightest star here; the whole constellation has only two stars readily visible.

Capricornus is the Sea-Goat, a creature with a goat's body and fish's tail — the god Pan who dived into the Nile to escape the monster Typhon. Its stars form a wide triangle; the Sun passes through in January.

Carina was once part of the giant ship Argo Navis, sailed by Jason and the Argonauts. It holds Canopus, the second-brightest star in the sky, and Eta Carinae, a doomed star over 100 times the Sun's mass.

Cassiopeia the Queen sits strapped to her throne in the sky as punishment for her vanity — her circumpolar stars circle the pole forever, sometimes hanging upside down. Her 'W' shape makes her one of the easiest constellations to spot.
Centaurus is the centaur Chiron, teacher of heroes like Achilles. It holds Proxima Centauri, the closest star to the Sun, at just 4.2 light years, plus the beautiful globular cluster Omega Centauri.
Cepheus was the King of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. Its delta star is the original Cepheid — a 'standard candle' star whose pulse revealed the size of the universe.

Cetus is the sea monster sent to devour Andromeda. It contains Mira, 'the wonderful', a star that swells and fades over 11 months, and hosts the first extrasolar planet candidates ever studied in detail.
Chamaeleon, 'the Chameleon', lies near the south celestial pole. Its galaxies are shielded from southern sky clutter; it contains clouds where new stars are being born.
Pyxis is the Mariner's Compass, a relic of Argo Navis carved off in the 1840s. Its star T Pyxidis is a recurrent nova, erupting every few decades.
Columba was created by Petrus Plancius in 1592 as the dove of Noah's ark. Its star Wazn ('the weight') is tiny — a star barely half the Sun's mass that still shines as a visible orange star.

Coma Berenices honours Queen Berenice II of Egypt, who cut her hair as an offering to Aphrodite — the lost locks were 'found' in the sky by the astronomer Conon. The Coma Cluster here holds more than a thousand galaxies.
Corona Australis, the Southern Crown, is a small arc of stars marking a wreath for a southern god. It contains a dark cloud, the Coronet, where a clutch of baby stars is forming.

Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown, represents a crown given by Dionysus to Ariadne. Its gem is Alphecca, and the constellation contains a famous recurring nova called T Coronae Borealis, the 'Blaze Star'.
Corvus the Crow was sent by Apollo to fetch water in a cup but dawdled, blaming a snake — Apollo punished all three with their places in the sky. The four stars form a distinctive kite shape.
Crater is the cup of Apollo, sitting on the back of the snake Hydra in the sky. Its stars are all faint; the constellation's shape, a goblet, is surprisingly easy to pick out.

Crux, the Southern Cross, is the smallest constellation but one of the most famous — it appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil and others. It sits in the richest part of the Milky Way.
Cygnus the Swan flies along the Milky Way; its brightest star Deneb anchors the Summer Triangle. The star system Cygnus X-1 here was the first black hole ever identified.
Delphinus is a small but charming constellation shaped like a dolphin leaping. In old seafaring lore it rescued the poet Arion of Lesbos from drowning.
Dorado, 'the dolphinfish', contains the Tarantula Nebula, the most active star-forming region in our cosmic neighbourhood — and hosted Supernova 1987A, the nearest supernova in four centuries.
Draco the Dragon coils between the two Bears, with its head near Hercules. The star Thuban, in Draco's tail, was the pole star 4,000 years ago when the Egyptian pyramids were built.
Equuleus, 'the Little Horse' or foal, is the second-smallest constellation. It has no stars brighter than 4th magnitude and was possibly invented by Hipparchus in the 2nd century BC.
Eridanus is the River of heaven, sixth-largest of all constellations. Its bright star Achernar is the most oblate star known — spinning so fast it's flattened like a tangerine.
Fornax, 'the Furnace', was named by Lacaille. It is home to the Fornax Cluster of galaxies and to the famous Hubble Deep Field, where the telescope stared for days into 'empty' space.
Gemini represents the twins Castor and Pollux, the patron twins of sailors who appeared as St Elmo's fire. The Geminid meteor shower, one of the year's best, radiates from here each December.
Grus, the Crane, was carved out of Pavo's area by Dutch navigators around 1600. Its brightest star, Alnair, means 'the bright one from the fish's tail' in Arabic.
Hercules is the Greek hero kneeling with club raised, celebrating his Twelve Labours. His head holds the 'Keystone' — four stars forming the famous asterism within which lies the Great Cluster M13.
Horologium, 'the Clock', was named by Lacaille to honour the pendulum clock invented by Christiaan Huygens. It contains the 'El Gordo' galaxy cluster, one of the largest known in the universe.
Hydra is the largest constellation in the sky, winding over 100 degrees from Cancer to Centaurus. Its head contains the wide double star Alphard, 'the solitary one', an orange giant shining alone.
Hydrus, the Lesser Water Snake, is a southern companion to Hydra. It was charted around 1600 by Keyser and de Houtman and sits near the Magellanic Clouds.

Indus, 'the Indian', was named for the people of the East and West Indies encountered by Dutch explorers. It contains no bright stars, but its naked-eye ellipticals hold an unusual concentration of globular clusters.
Lacerta, 'the Lizard', was created by Johannes Hevelius in 1687 to fill a gap between Cygnus and Andromeda. It contains the 'Blaze Star' BL Lacertae, prototype of an entire class of active galaxies.

Leo the Lion is one of the oldest recognised constellations. Its bright star Regulus lies almost exactly on the Sun's path, so the Sun and Moon pass right by it. The Leonid meteors storm from here every November.
Leo Minor was created by Johannes Hevelius in 1687 to fill a space between the Lion and the Great Bear. It has no star brighter than 4th magnitude — a 'sky filler' with almost no famous objects.
Lepus the Hare crouches at Orion's feet, fleeing his hunting dogs. It contains the wonderful Eskimo Nebula, an aging star blowing off its outer layers into a shell shaped like a face.

Libra is the only constellation of the zodiac that isn't a person or animal — it's the Scales of Justice. The Greeks once saw it as the claws of the Scorpion; its star names mean 'northern claw' and 'southern claw' to this day.
Lupus, the Wolf, was 'the Beast' to the Greeks, sacrificed by the Centaur. The star cluster NGC 5822 lies here, and the supernova of 1006 — the brightest ever recorded — exploded nearby in history.
Lynx is so faint that Hevelius quipped only a lynx-eyed observer could spot it. Its brightest star, Alpha Lyncis, is a red giant 200 light years away.
Lyra is the lyre of Orpheus, whose music could charm stones and beasts. Its star Vega was the northern pole star around 12,000 BC — and will be again in another 12,000 years.
Mensa, 'the Table Mountain', was named by Lacaille from the flat mountain near Cape Town where he observed. It contains no star brighter than 5th magnitude but lies beside the Large Magellanic Cloud.

Microscopium, 'the Microscope', is one of Lacaille's scientific instruments. Its stars are faint, but the constellation contains a remarkable group of galaxies photographed by the James Webb Space Telescope.
Monoceros, the Unicorn, was created by Petrus Plancius in 1613. Its stars are faint, but the constellation hides the Rosette Nebula and Hubble's Variable Nebula.

Musca, 'the Fly', was originally called 'the Bee' — and 'the Southern Fly' — before settling on the insect we know. It lies near the Southern Cross and contains the famous binary system with a black hole.
Norma, 'the Carpenter's Level', is another Lacaille instrument. It sits toward the centre of the Milky Way, packed with star clouds and nebulae.
Octans, 'the Octant', was named by Lacaille for the navigational instrument — and it contains the south celestial pole itself. The star sigma Octantis is the faint, hard-to-spot southern pole star.

Ophiuchus the Serpent Bearer represents Asclepius, the god of medicine, holding the snake that taught him healing. In 2016 NASA jokingly pointed out the Sun spends 18 days here — making it the '13th zodiac sign'.

Orion the Hunter is the most recognisable constellation in the sky, with its three-star belt and brilliant Betelgeuse and Rigel. The Orion Nebula, hanging from his belt, is a stellar nursery visible to the naked eye.
Pavo, the Peacock, was charted by Dutch navigators around 1600. Its brightest star, simply called Peacock, is a double star; the constellation also hosts the naked-eye globular cluster NGC 6752.

Pegasus, the Winged Horse, sprang from the blood of Medusa when Perseus beheaded her. The 'Great Square' of Pegasus is a famous autumn landmark; its star 51 Pegasi hosted the first exoplanet found around a Sun-like star.
Perseus the Hero carries the severed head of Medusa — the blinking star Algiers' 'Demon Star', Algol, represents her eye. The famous Perseid meteor shower every August comes from this constellation.
Phoenix, the Firebird, was charted by Dutch navigators around 1600. It contains a naked-eye globular cluster and the star Ankaa, 'the Phoenix', an orange giant.
Pictor, 'the Painter's Easel', was one of Lacaille's inventions. The star Beta Pictoris here has a famous circumstellar disk — one of the first disks ever photographed, containing newborn planets.

Pisces represents the goddesses Aphrodite and her son Eros who turned into fish to escape the monster Typhon. The Sun enters the zodiac here at the March equinox; it holds the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star found, and M74, the 'Phantom Galaxy'.
Piscis Austrinus, the Southern Fish, holds the bright star Fomalhaut, 'the mouth of the fish' — one of the twenty brightest stars. Fomalhaut has one of the most photographed disks of dust in the sky.
Puppis is the stern of the great ship Argo. It contains several open clusters and was split off from Argo Navis in the 1840s, along with Carina and Vela.
Pyxis is the Mariner's Compass, a relic of Argo Navis carved off in the 1840s. Its star T Pyxidis is a recurrent nova, erupting every few decades.

Reticulum, 'the Reticle' or eyepiece grid of a telescope, was named by Lacaille. It has no bright stars but contains the double star Zeta Reticuli, famous in UFO lore for an alleged alien abduction map.
Sagitta, the Arrow, is the third-smallest constellation. The Greeks saw it as Apollo's arrow, shot to kill the Cyclopes; its arrow-shaped asterism is easy to find.
Sagittarius the Archer is a centaur drawing his bow toward Scorpius. His arrow points at the centre of the Milky Way — the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A* lies in this direction.

Scorpius the Scorpion killed Orion with its sting, and the two were placed on opposite sides of the sky so they'd never meet again. Its heart is Antares, 'rival of Mars', a red giant 700 times the Sun's diameter.

Sculptor, 'the Sculptor's Studio', was named by Lacaille. It lies away from the Milky Way in a clear gap — ideal for spotting distant galaxies, including the Sculptor Dwarf, one of our Galaxy's nearest satellites.
Scutum, 'the Shield', was created by Johannes Hevelius in 1687 and named for King John Sobieski of Poland. Its most famous object is the Wild Duck Cluster, a compact flock of young stars.

Serpens Cauda is the tail of the serpent held by Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer — Serpens is the only constellation divided into two pieces. Its tail contains the Eagle Nebula, home of the famous 'Pillars of Creation'.

Serpens Cauda is the tail of the serpent held by Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer — Serpens is the only constellation divided into two pieces. Its tail contains the Eagle Nebula, home of the famous 'Pillars of Creation'.
Sextans, 'the Sextant', was named by Johannes Hevelius after the instrument he used for his star catalogue. Its stars are faint; it lies between the Lion and the Hydra.

Taurus the Bull is one of the oldest constellations, painted in Paleolithic caves. Its V-shaped face is the Hyades cluster; the bright red star Aldebaran marks the Bull's eye, and the Pleiades shine on his shoulder.

Telescopium, 'the Telescope', was one of Lacaille's instrument constellations. Its brightest star is a mere 4th magnitude; the constellation points at the Milky Way's centre and hosts a giant gamma-ray structure called the 'Fermi Bubbles' region.

Triangulum, 'the Triangle', was one of Ptolemy's original 48 constellations, representing the Nile Delta or the island of Sicily. It contains the Triangulum Galaxy, the third-largest member of our Local Group.
Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle, was charted by Dutch navigators around 1600. Its brightest star, Atria, is a red giant 400 light years away.

Tucana, the Toucan, was charted by Dutch navigators around 1600. It contains the Small Magellanic Cloud's star clusters, including the beautiful globular 47 Tucanae — the second-brightest globular in the sky.

Ursa Major, the Great Bear, contains the Big Dipper, the most famous star pattern in the northern sky. The Dipper's two outer stars point the way to Polaris; the middle stars of the handle are actually a real double system.
Ursa Minor, the Little Bear, contains Polaris, the North Star, at the tip of its handle. Polaris is a Cepheid variable and a triple system; it has guided navigators for centuries.
Vela is the sails of the great ship Argo Navis. It contains the Gum Nebula, the largest known expanding nebula, and the beautiful 'False Cross' asterism shared with Carina.
Virgo the Maiden is the second-largest constellation, and one of the oldest. It holds the Virgo Cluster, more than 1,300 galaxies, and the bright star Spica, 'the ear of wheat' in the Maiden's hand.
Volans, 'the Flying Fish', was charted by Dutch navigators around 1600. It has no bright stars but lies near the rich Carina region, with a pretty pair of open clusters.
Vulpecula, 'the Little Fox', was created by Johannes Hevelius in 1687, originally as 'the Fox and the Goose'. It holds the Dumbbell Nebula, the first planetary nebula ever discovered.
